vt.analysis:
Type: OpenClaw Skill
Name: certcheck
Version: 1.0.4

The skill bundle exhibits a critical discrepancy between its documentation and implementation: SKILL.md describes a comprehensive SSL/TLS certificate analysis tool, but scripts/script.sh is actually a generic JSON-based entry manager (CRUD app) with no network or SSL capabilities. Additionally, the script contains a code injection vulnerability in the cmd_config function, where the CERTCHECK_DIR environment variable is unsafely interpolated into a python3 -c command string. This combination of misleading instructions for the AI agent and a functional mismatch suggests either a highly malformed package or an intentional attempt to provide a 'bait-and-switch' capability.

llm.summary: The skill's description promises SSL/TLS certificate inspection, but the included code is a local entry-management CLI that does not perform any certificate checks — this mismatch is concerning and should be clarified before installing.

dimensions.detail: The skill claims to be an SSL/TLS certificate checker (check, expiry, chain, batch), but the bundled script implements a local entries manager (init, add, list, show, remove, search, export, stats, config, status, reset). There are no network, TLS, or certificate-parsing operations (no openssl/curl/s_client, no Python TLS library usage). The requested files and behavior do not align with the stated purpose.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: SKILL.md documents certificate-related commands that the runtime instructions would be expected to run, but the runtime script does not implement them. The script does create and manipulate files under the user's data directory (default ~/.local/share/certcheck/), including a reset command that can delete those files. While the script does not exfiltrate data or call external endpoints, the instructions are misleading and grant the agent broad discretion to read/write/delete local data in the user's home directory.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: There is no install spec (instruction-only), which is low risk in itself. However, a code file (scripts/script.sh) is included but there is no guidance on how it becomes the 'certcheck' command; this mismatch increases user confusion and may lead to manual, ad-hoc placement of the script into PATH. No downloads or external installers are used.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The script optionally honors CERTCHECK_DIR to change its data directory; no secret environment variables or unrelated credentials are requested. The script's access to a data directory in the user's home is proportionate for a local CLI, but note that it will create, modify, and can delete files there.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill does not request permanent platform-wide inclusion (always: false) and does not modify other skills or system-wide configurations. It writes to and manages files only in its own data directory.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: Do not install or run this skill assuming it will check TLS certificates — the included script does not implement any certificate-checking functionality and appears to be a simple local note/entry manager. Before installing: (1) verify the author/source (BytesAgain / bytesagain.com) and confirm whether you received the correct package; (2) inspect the script yourself — it will create ~/.local/share/certcheck/ by default and the 'reset' command can delete that data; (3) if you expected TLS checks, use a reputable tool (openssl s_client, sslscan, or well-known libraries) or ask the publisher for the real certcheck implementation; (4) if you still want to try this package, run it in an isolated environment (container or VM) and do not run destructive commands until you've backed up data. The main issue is a functional mismatch (mislabeling or packaging error), not explicit exfiltration, but the discrepancy is significant enough to warrant caution.
